edit_from_base: append 'and easing on the transitions' to base phrase
prompt: Animate the player (idle, run, jump, fall) using an AnimationTree with a state machine and easing on the transitions.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Review player.gd and the Player scene to see how movement, jumping, and gravity are currently handled, and note which signals (velocity, is_on_floor) can drive the four animation states.
2. Prepare the sprite art for idle, run, jump, and fall, either as a spritesheet on the Sprite2D (set up frames/hframes) or as separate frames, and confirm the pixel-art import settings so it stays crisp.
3. Add an AnimationPlayer to the Player scene and create one animation per state (idle, run, jump, fall), keying the sprite frame track, setting loop modes, and choosing frame timing.
4. Add an AnimationTree node, point it at the AnimationPlayer, and set its root to an AnimationNodeStateMachine with the four animations as states.
5. Define the transitions between states (idle to run, run to idle, any grounded state to jump, jump to fall, fall to idle or run) with switch modes, conditions or expressions, and an xfade time plus an easing curve on each transition.
6. Update player.gd to activate the tree and feed it each physics frame with the inputs it needs (horizontal speed, vertical velocity, grounded state), and flip the sprite based on facing direction.
7. Playtest in level_01.tscn, checking every transition (landing, walking off ledges, jump at the apex, quick direction changes) and tuning xfade times and easing so blends feel responsive rather than floaty.
8. Clean up by removing any old direct animation-play calls from player.gd and confirming the enemy scenes and other levels are unaffected.

1. Prepare the animation frames: confirm the player's Sprite2D sheet has idle, run, jump and fall frames, and set up the frame grid (hframes/vframes or a SpriteFrames resource) so each pose can be addressed.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer as a child of Player and author four animations (idle, run, jump, fall), setting loop on idle and run and keeping jump and fall as short or held poses.
3. Add an AnimationTree node under Player, point it at the AnimationPlayer, and set its root to a state machine.
4. Create the four states in the state machine (idle, run, jump, fall) and assign each one to its matching animation.
5. Draw the transitions between states (idle to run, run to idle, any ground state to jump, jump to fall, fall to idle or run on landing) and set each to switch at the right moment, such as at the end of the clip for landing.
6. Give every transition a cross-fade time and an easing curve so poses blend smoothly, using short, snappy fades for jump and landing and slightly longer ones for idle and run.
7. Update player.gd to drive the tree: fetch the state machine playback and send it the current state each physics frame based on floor contact, horizontal input and vertical velocity, and flip the sprite to match facing direction.
8. Playtest in level_01.tscn, checking that there are no flicker or stuck states on ledges, coyote jumps or landings, then tune the blend times and easing curves until it feels right.

1. Prepare the sprite sheet assets for idle, run, jump, and fall, and import them with pixel-art-friendly texture settings. Set the Sprite2D frame layout (hframes/vframes) so each animation maps to a clear frame range.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer to the Player scene and author four animations (idle, run, jump, fall) that key the Sprite2D frame property. Set loop modes: idle and run loop, jump and fall hold or loop their last frames.
3. Add an AnimationTree node to the Player scene, point it at the AnimationPlayer, and set its root to an AnimationNodeStateMachine. Keep it inactive until the graph is wired.
4. Build the state machine graph with idle, run, jump, and fall states, and an entry to idle. Add the transitions between them (idle to run, run to idle, any grounded state to jump, jump to fall, fall to idle or run on landing).
5. Configure each transition with a switch mode, an advance condition, and an easing: set the xfade time and easing curve per transition, shorter for jump and fall, longer for idle and run. Use a blend-friendly curve so the pose changes do not snap.
6. Expose the conditions in player.gd by feeding the AnimationTree from the movement state each physics frame: grounded, horizontal speed, and vertical velocity sign. Also flip the Sprite2D based on facing direction, and activate the tree on ready.
7. Verify in level_01.tscn by running the scene and exercising each state: standing, running, jumping, falling off a ledge, and landing. Check that no transition flickers, such as running-to-falling on slopes or tile seams, and tune the conditions and xfade times.
8. Review the transitions for edge cases like coyote time, double jump, or taking damage, and make sure the enemy scenes are unaffected. Save the Player scene and commit the changes.

1. Audit player.gd and the Player scene to see how movement, jumping, and gravity are currently handled, and which signals or properties (velocity, is_on_floor, facing direction) can drive animation. Confirm the Sprite2D's sprite sheet frame layout for idle, run, jump, and fall.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer to the Player scene and create four animations (idle, run, jump, fall) that key the Sprite2D frames, with looping set for idle and run and one-shot or hold behavior for jump and fall.
3. Add an AnimationTree node pointing at the AnimationPlayer, set its root to an AnimationNodeStateMachine, and leave it inactive until it is configured.
4. In the state machine, add the four animation states, set idle as the start state, and wire the transitions: idle to run, run to idle, idle or run to jump, jump to fall, fall to idle or run, and idle or run to fall for walking off ledges.
5. Configure each transition with a sensible switch mode, advance condition or expression, and an easing curve with a short cross-fade time (for example a quick ease-in-out for ground transitions and a snappier one for jump and fall) so poses blend smoothly.
6. Update player.gd to grab the AnimationTree's playback object and set the conditions or parameters each physics frame from velocity and floor state, plus flip the sprite based on horizontal direction, without changing the existing movement logic.
7. Activate the AnimationTree and run level_01.tscn to test every transition, including landing, ledge falls, and quick direction changes, watching for flicker or stuck states.
8. Tune the easing curves, blend times, and animation speeds based on playtesting, then verify the enemy scenes and level are unaffected and save the scene changes.

1. Prepare the sprite art: confirm the player spritesheet has idle, run, jump and fall frames, and set up the Sprite2D with the correct hframes/vframes (or switch to AnimatedSprite2D) so each state maps to a clear frame range.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer under the Player scene and author four animations (idle, run, jump, fall) that key the sprite frames, with looping on idle and run and no looping on jump and fall.
3. Add an AnimationTree node pointing at the AnimationPlayer, set its tree root to an AnimationNodeStateMachine, and leave it inactive until the graph is complete.
4. In the state machine, create the four states (idle, run, jump, fall) with idle as the start node, and draw transitions between them (idle<->run, idle/run->jump, jump->fall, fall->idle/run, and so on).
5. Configure each transition's easing: set a short xfade time and an easing curve (for example ease-in-out) on transitions, and choose switch modes (immediate for jump, at-end where an animation should finish) so changes blend smoothly.
6. Drive the transitions from player.gd by reading velocity and is_on_floor() each physics frame, then travelling the state machine playback to idle, run, jump or fall, and flip the sprite horizontally based on movement direction.
7. Activate the AnimationTree, remove or replace any existing direct animation or frame-setting code in player.gd, and make sure state changes are not requested redundantly every frame.
8. Playtest in level_01.tscn across ground, platforms and ledge drops, checking for flicker, stuck states or abrupt cuts, then tune xfade times, easing curves and transition conditions until the motion feels right.

1. Prepare the animation source: confirm the Sprite2D uses a sprite sheet (or add one) and decide on the frame regions for idle, run, jump, and fall, keeping the Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D as they are.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer to the Player scene and create four animations (idle, run, jump, fall) that drive the Sprite2D frames, with looping on idle and run and no looping on jump and fall.
3. Add an AnimationTree node to the Player scene, point it at the AnimationPlayer, and set its root to an AnimationNodeStateMachine, leaving it inactive until it is fully wired.
4. In the state machine, add the four animation states and define the start state (idle) plus the allowed transitions: idle to run, run to idle, idle or run to jump, jump to fall, and fall to idle or run.
5. Configure each transition with a crossfade (xfade) time and an easing curve, choosing short fades for run/idle and snappier ones for jump/fall, and set the switch mode (immediate or at-end) per transition.
6. Update player.gd to read the playback object from the AnimationTree and drive it each physics frame from velocity and is_on_floor(): travel to idle, run, jump, or fall, and flip the sprite based on horizontal direction.
7. Activate the AnimationTree and make sure the AnimationPlayer's own autoplay does not conflict with it, then tune the transition times and curves while playing level_01.tscn.
8. Test edge cases in level_01.tscn, such as walking off ledges, landing, jumping while running, and rapid direction changes, and verify the enemy scenes are unaffected.
